Q: How are Recall@K, Precision@K, and MRR calculated?
A:
**Retrieval metrics describe a ranking relative to declared relevance labels.** For top-k unique retrieved IDs R and relevant IDs G, Recall@k=|R intersect G|/|G| and Precision@k=|R intersect G|/|R| when R is the returned top-k set. State whether a fixed-k denominator is used instead; do not switch conventions between systems. Reciprocal rank is 1/r for the first relevant hit at rank r, or zero if none. MRR averages reciprocal rank across a declared query set.

For graded relevance g_i at rank i, one common DCG is sum((2^g_i-1)/log2(i+1)); nDCG divides by the ideal DCG from the same labels. Declare the gain convention. With binary relevance, one relevant item at rank 2 has Recall=1, RR=1/2 and nDCG=1/log2(3), approximately 0.63093. If two gold items exist but only one is retrieved, recall is 1/2 even if that item ranks first. A duplicate relevant ID must not count twice.

**Unanswerable queries need a different oracle.** An empty gold set makes recall undefined rather than automatically perfect. Report it as not applicable and evaluate correct abstention or unsupported-answer rate. Missing labels are not proof of irrelevance: pool candidate results from several methods, adjudicate scope/revision/claim applicability and record disagreement. Keep question IDs stable and group near-duplicates by document/customer/time when splitting data so copied examples do not leak across train, tuning and held-out evaluation.

`policy_assistant_project.py` fixes case IDs and gold answer spans independently of prediction. Its arithmetic test checks rank-two nDCG against a hand-calculated constant, and its deliberate missing-exception regression must fail. The fixture is small and English-only; 8/8 is not an estimate of broad production accuracy. Report counts and per-case outcomes, not a misleading confidence claim. On a larger release set, compare paired old/new outcomes on identical queries, inspect critical regressions and use uncertainty methods appropriate to correlated cases rather than treating every paraphrase as an independent customer.
Why: For ranking [noise,gold], binary relevance gives Recall=1, RR=0.5 and nDCG approximately 0.63093. The independent arithmetic oracle would catch an implementation that incorrectly uses rank zero or duplicate hits.
Risk: A label set that ignores owner or revision can reward a forbidden result. Averaging unanswerable recall as one inflates quality without improving any answer.
Trade: MRR emphasizes the first relevant hit, while nDCG captures position and graded relevance. Neither measures whether the final answer follows the evidence or whether latency is acceptable.
Try: Write the three metric formulas before running the capstone. Change a prediction to rank the gold span second, then duplicate the ID and verify that malformed ranking is rejected rather than rewarded.

follow_ups.Q: What if experts disagree whether a passage is relevant?
follow_ups.A: Record the disagreement, question conditions and adjudication rule. Evaluate sensitivity under plausible labels or graded relevance; do not hide uncertain labels behind a falsely exact benchmark score.

Q: How should I create a useful evaluation dataset?
A: A production-grade RAG evaluation dataset cannot rely on a trivial collection of happy-path QA pairs. It requires a structured, multi-dimensional benchmark schema built on four core principles: (1) Four-Category Query Taxonomy: Benchmark suites must include: (a) Explicit factual lookups requiring single-document extraction; (b) Multi-hop queries requiring synthesis across disparate documents; (c) Paraphrased and noisy queries reflecting real-world user typos and conversational shorthand; and (d) Deliberately unanswerable or out-of-domain queries to test system refusal and abstention boundaries; (2) Rich Ground-Truth Annotations: Each evaluation instance must capture: query ID, exact query text, authoritative gold document/chunk IDs, acceptable answer variations, atomic claim decompositions, and explicit authorization/tenant metadata; (3) Strict Entity-Based Split Isolation: To prevent catastrophic data leakage, train/tuning/test partitions must be partitioned by source document and subject entity rather than random sampling. If a model fine-tunes embeddings or prompts on Document A, testing on paraphrases of Document A produces wildly inflated scores that collapse in production; and (4) Temporal Versioning: Labeled datasets must be bound to immutable corpus snapshots (`corpus_git_hash` or `corpus_version_id`), ensuring that updates to company policies do not invalidate historic evaluation baselines.
Why: Randomly splitting QA pairs across train and test sets allows lexical and semantic leakage from shared source documents, producing misleading benchmark scores that fail to generalize to real users.
Risk: Omitting unanswerable queries from evaluation datasets creates a false benchmark where models that hallucinate confident falsehoods score higher than models that correctly abstain.
Trade: Authoring expert-verified ground truth with atomic claims and entity-isolated splits requires significant human engineering effort, but provides the only reliable baseline for production release gating.
Try: Construct a 50-query evaluation set containing 10 multi-hop queries and 10 unanswerable queries partitioned strictly by document domain; verify that evaluation metrics isolate abstention accuracy from extraction recall.

Q: Why is retrieval-only evaluation useful before generation exists?
A: Retrieval-only evaluation isolates the search component as an independent subsystem before introducing the latency, cost, and non-determinism of generative LLMs: (1) Performance Ceiling Determination: In any RAG pipeline, downstream generation quality is strictly bounded by retrieval recall. If the gold evidence is not retrieved within top-K candidates (`Recall@K = 0`), the generator must either hallucinate or abstain. Evaluating retrieval first identifies whether failure originates in search or in generation; (2) Deterministic, Cost-Effective Optimization: Retrieval metrics (Hit@K, Precision@K, NDCG@K, MRR) run completely offline in milliseconds using deterministic math, with zero LLM API costs or token rate limits. This enables rapid hyperparameter sweeps across chunk sizes (256 vs 512 vs 1024 tokens), chunk overlap, embedding models, and hybrid search weights (BM25 vs dense vector ratios); and (3) Reranking & Context Window Budgeting: Isolating retrieval reveals whether adding an expensive Cross-Encoder reranker justifies its latency cost by measuring the delta in `MRR@10` against raw vector search, and ensures only high-signal passages consume LLM context budget.
Why: Evaluating only end-to-end generated answers obscures the root cause of failures: an incorrect answer could be caused by bad retrieval, poor context packing, or generator hallucination.
Risk: Optimizing generation prompts when retrieval recall is poor wastes engineering hours tuning system instructions to compensate for missing or noisy context.
Trade: Retrieval-only benchmarks do not test whether the generator can synthesize complex multi-document reasoning, but establish the prerequisite foundation required for generation to succeed.
Try: Benchmark BM25 alone, dense embeddings alone, and reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) on a labeled query set; measure NDCG@10 and identify which queries fail across all retrieval modes.

Q: How do heuristic answer scoring and LLM-as-judge differ?
A: Evaluating generated answers requires understanding the fundamental trade-offs between deterministic heuristic scoring and probabilistic LLM judges: (1) Heuristic Scoring (Exact Match, BLEU, ROUGE-L, F1-token): Computes n-gram overlap between generated text and ground-truth answers. They are free, execute in microseconds, and provide stable CI/CD regression baselines. However, they suffer severe lexical brittleness: valid semantic paraphrases receive near-zero scores, while fluent answers that parrot reference text without answering the prompt receive falsely high scores; (2) LLM-as-a-Judge (e.g. GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, G-Eval): Prompts a powerful model to grade answers on structured dimensions (Faithfulness, Answer Relevance, Completeness, Conciseness) using calibrated rubrics. Judges capture nuanced semantic equivalence and factual entailment, but introduce non-determinism, significant API costs, latency, and cognitive biases (position bias, verbosity bias, and self-enhancement bias toward their own model family); and (3) Production Hybrid Architecture: Modern pipelines use deterministic heuristics for formatting, length, and keyword constraints, fine-tuned lightweight NLI models (e.g. DeBERTa-v3) for factual entailment verification, and calibrated LLM judges (validated with Cohen's Kappa against human expert ratings) for qualitative dimensions.
Why: Relying solely on lexical heuristics fails to evaluate semantic accuracy, while uncalibrated LLM judges introduce hidden biases and non-deterministic scoring shifts into evaluation pipelines.
Risk: Deploying an LLM judge without position-bias mitigation (swapping candidate order) or verbosity penalties allows verbose, hallucinated answers to outscore concise, accurate answers.
Trade: Heuristics provide cheap, reproducible regression gates for CI/CD; LLM judges provide human-correlated evaluation but require careful calibration, caching, and temperature=0 configurations.
Try: Evaluate three candidate answers (exact match, fluent paraphrase, and hallucination with high word overlap) using both ROUGE-L and an LLM judge; observe the failure modes of each scoring mechanism.

Q: What does a high-value test strategy look like for this reference design?
A: A high-value testing strategy for production RAG and AI systems follows a decoupled seam-based architecture that separates deterministic code logic from non-deterministic model behavior: (1) Seam Unit Tests with In-Memory Fakes: Fast, deterministic unit tests verify tokenizers, chunking boundary logic, metadata extractors, and SSE streaming parsers. All external LLM and embedding API clients are stubbed using deterministic in-memory fakes to ensure test suites execute in seconds without network dependencies; (2) Integration & Concurrency Tests with Testcontainers: Test PostgreSQL/pgvector queries, Redis distributed locks, RLS security policies, and CAS status updates against real containerized services. Verifies that race conditions, connection pool timeouts, and rollback semantics behave correctly under concurrency; (3) Hermetic Evaluation Regression Gates: Automated CI/CD pipelines run frozen offline evaluation datasets against candidate embedding and prompt configurations, enforcing strict threshold gates on NDCG@10, faithfulness, and zero forbidden-data disclosures; and (4) End-to-End Browser & Chaos Tests: Playwright suites test full client journeys over actual compiled web bundles, injecting network drops, chunk fragmentation, and mid-stream cancellation tokens to verify client state machine recovery.
Why: Testing AI applications solely through end-to-end live model calls creates slow, expensive, and flaky CI pipelines that fail to isolate where regressions occur.
Risk: Relying on in-memory mocks for database concurrency or RLS policies hides deadlocks, race conditions, and cross-tenant data leaks that only manifest against real relational engines.
Trade: Maintaining containerized integration tests and deterministic fakes requires explicit test infrastructure setup, but guarantees reliable, reproducible builds across the team.
Try: Write an integration test using Testcontainers that attempts two concurrent document updates under a fencing token; assert that exactly one succeeds and the other triggers an optimistic lock exception.

Q: What is the difference between liveness, readiness, and degraded health?
A: In cloud-native AI services running on Kubernetes or container orchestrators, health monitoring must decouple three distinct operational states: (1) Liveness (`/healthz/liveness`): Answers 'Is the process runtime healthy, or has it entered an unrecoverable deadlock or thread hang?' If the liveness probe fails, Kubernetes terminates and restarts the container. Liveness probes must be extremely lightweight (e.g. checking local event loop responsiveness) and must NEVER depend on downstream external databases or APIs; (2) Readiness (`/healthz/readiness`): Answers 'Can this specific container pod accept incoming production queries right now?' Checks active database connection pool availability, local vector index memory warming, and local model socket readiness. If readiness fails, the pod is removed from the load balancer pool without being terminated; and (3) Degraded Health (`/healthz/status`): The service is operational but running under impaired capabilities: e.g., the primary vector database replica is down and queries have fallen back to a read-only secondary, background document re-indexing is lagging by >1 hour, or the GPU reranker is saturated and the service has temporarily fallen back to BM25-only retrieval.
Why: Conflating liveness with database readiness causes cascading container restart storms: if PostgreSQL has a temporary blip, killing all healthy API pods worsens cluster exhaustion.
Risk: Including slow database queries or vector similarity searches in liveness probes causes Kubernetes to kill busy workers under high load, turning a transient traffic spike into a complete outage.
Trade: Exposing granular liveness, readiness, and degraded endpoints requires explicit health probe design, but enables zero-downtime rolling deploys and automatic traffic shedding.
Try: Simulate a database connection pool exhaustion; assert that `/healthz/readiness` returns 503 (removing the pod from routing) while `/healthz/liveness` returns 200 (preventing restart thrashing).

Q: What operational signals should be monitored?
A: Production observability for RAG systems requires full-stack telemetry combining infrastructure metrics, application pipeline stages, and domain-specific quality signals: (1) Pipeline Stage Latencies: Track p50, p95, and p99 durations across distinct spans via OpenTelemetry: Query Rewrite latency, Vector Index Search latency, Cross-Encoder Rerank latency, Prompt Assembly latency, and Time to First Token (TTFT); (2) Retrieval & Evidence Quality: Monitor empty retrieval rates (queries returning zero chunks), average vector distance distributions, evidence truncation frequency (chunks dropped due to context budget limits), and retrieval cache hit ratios; (3) Generation & Provider Metrics: Monitor token consumption (prompt tokens vs completion tokens per turn), streaming inter-token latency, provider rate limit headroom (429 status codes), and prompt cache hit rates; and (4) Safety, Guardrails & User Feedback: Track guardrail intervention frequency (input prompt injections blocked, output PII redactions triggered), explicit user feedback ratios (thumbs up vs thumbs down per tenant), and model abstention/refusal frequency.
Why: Monitoring only HTTP status codes and CPU usage blinds operators to silent degradation: an API returning HTTP 200 can be serving empty retrievals, truncated contexts, or hallucinated answers.
Risk: Attaching high-cardinality metadata (e.g. raw user prompts, document IDs, or raw query text) to Prometheus metrics causes metric server OOMs and leaks sensitive PII into monitoring logs.
Trade: Emitting detailed OpenTelemetry spans for every RAG turn adds slight network and storage overhead for tracing collectors, but enables instant diagnosis of latency spikes and retrieval degradation.
Try: Set up OpenTelemetry spans for retrieval, reranking, and generation; simulate a slow embedding endpoint and observe how distributed trace waterfalls pinpoint the bottleneck.

Q: How should a system meet an end-to-end latency target?
A: Meeting aggressive end-to-end latency targets (e.g., TTFT < 800ms, total completion < 2500ms) in RAG systems requires strict latency budgeting and asynchronous parallel execution: (1) Stage-by-Stage Latency Budgeting: Allocate deterministic time budgets to every pipeline hop: Auth & Gateway (30ms) -> Query Expansion (80ms) -> Hybrid Vector/BM25 Search (150ms) -> Cross-Encoder Reranker (150ms) -> Context Assembly (40ms) -> LLM TTFT (300ms) -> Network buffer margin (50ms); (2) Concurrent Stage Execution: Run sparse lexical search (BM25) and dense embedding vector search concurrently via `asyncio.gather()`, rather than executing them sequentially; (3) Context Caching & Speculative Reranking: Leverage LLM prompt caching (e.g. Anthropic prompt caching or OpenAI cached tokens) for static system instructions and documentation context, reducing TTFT by up to 70%; (4) Dynamic Load Shedding: Under high server concurrency, dynamically bypass non-essential stages: e.g., fall back from heavy Cross-Encoder reranking to fast Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), or reduce retrieved candidate count `k` from 50 to 10; and (5) Distributed Deadline Propagation: Propagate a `X-Request-Deadline` header across all microservices; if downstream retrieval exceeds its allocated budget, abort stale generation calls immediately.
Why: Executing RAG stages sequentially compounds latency: 200ms vector search + 250ms BM25 + 300ms reranking + 800ms generation exceeds interactive user patience thresholds before the first token appears.
Risk: Aggressive timeouts without deadline propagation leave backend vector searches or LLM inferences running after the client disconnects, wasting expensive compute resources.
Trade: Dynamically shedding the Cross-Encoder reranker during traffic spikes preserves interactive response times at the expense of a slight, acceptable dip in ranking precision.
Try: Implement an asynchronous pipeline running vector search and BM25 concurrently with a 200ms deadline; verify that if one search times out, the pipeline proceeds gracefully with the remaining candidates.

Q: How do you roll out a retrieval change safely?
A:
**A retrieval rollout is a controlled change to a measurable evidence path.** Offline evaluation compares candidate and baseline on the same frozen corpus, scope rules and labeled questions before traffic exposure. Online evaluation observes real product outcomes under an explicit allocation and privacy policy. A click or thumbs-up is not automatically a correctness label, and live experimentation cannot justify knowingly exposing private data or unsafe policy decisions.

Create a run manifest with code/configuration, source snapshot, embedding/reranker profiles, gold-set version and threshold policy. Report paired per-case changes: which supported answers improved, which became false refusals, which lost decisive evidence and whether any forbidden source appeared. Keep critical owner/citation failures as hard blockers independently of average relevance. Tune on development data; reserve a held-out release set so repeated threshold adjustments cannot memorize the acceptance answers.

**Trace the failure before changing the model.** A request timeline should distinguish queue wait, source search, reranking, context preparation, model first token and completion. Propagate request/attempt IDs and record safe source revision IDs, counts, stop reason and usage categories. Avoid raw prompts, document bodies and credentials in ordinary telemetry. Stage p95 values do not add into an end-to-end p95; measure the complete request distribution as well. A faster answer that omits the policy exception is a quality regression.

Deploy a reversible configuration/index version, shadow where appropriate without effects, then a limited canary with scope-aware quality, latency, cost and error budgets. Define sample requirements and rollback triggers in advance. Keep old artifacts compatible long enough for rollback; a schema migration or deleted-source restoration can make a naive rollback unsafe. The local capstone's missing-exception mutant demonstrates a regression gate: baseline passes, the candidate fails and the repaired candidate restores the required span. It proves that bounded fixture behavior, not actual customer success or production latency.
Why: A candidate returns faster because it excludes the final-sale exception. Baseline and candidate are scored on identical gold cases; the unsupported answer blocks release despite the latency improvement.
Risk: A mean quality gain can hide a severe minority or permission regression. Logging sensitive text to diagnose that regression can itself create another disclosure.
Trade: Shadow traffic avoids user-visible answers but still incurs cost and may send private data to a model. Canary exposure requires a safe task, explicit gates and a tested rollback path.
Try: Run the capstone baseline, deliberate regression and repair. Produce a release note listing changed cases, critical blockers, manifest hashes and a rollback decision; keep measured and proposed latency evidence separate.

follow_ups.Q: What if online success improves while the held-out policy cases regress?
follow_ups.A: Investigate metric mismatch and slice differences before promotion. Business engagement cannot overrule unauthorized disclosure or unsupported critical decisions; preserve the hard gate and obtain better representative labels.

Q: How should you investigate quality drift over time?
A: When production RAG answer quality degrades over time, diagnosing the regression requires systematic isolation across four independent drift vectors: (1) Corpus & Document Drift: Audit document ingestion logs for newly ingested, poorly formatted, or contradictory documents. Check whether outdated policies were properly tombstoned or if duplicate chunking created index pollution; (2) Query Distribution Drift: User search behavior evolves over time (e.g. new product launches, seasonal queries, emerging slang). Compute rolling 7-day embedding centroid shifts of user queries against the golden benchmark distribution to detect semantic drift; (3) Provider & Model Drift: Upstream cloud LLM APIs frequently update model weights, quantization levels, or safety guardrails behind stable model aliases. Run frozen benchmark prompts with `temperature=0` against the provider to detect silent behavioral changes; and (4) Vector Index Degradation: Check vector index parameters. In HNSW indexes, dynamic document additions and soft deletions cause index fragmentation, reducing graph connectivity and degrading recall over time unless periodic index rebuilds or vacuuming are performed.
Why: Assuming that quality degradation is always an LLM model issue leads teams to futile prompt engineering when the root cause is corrupted document ingestion or HNSW index fragmentation.
Risk: Failing to version document corpus snapshots alongside evaluation benchmarks makes it impossible to determine whether an answer score dropped due to pipeline bugs or updated source data.
Trade: Maintaining frozen regression benchmarks and tracking rolling embedding drift requires automated monitoring infrastructure, but enables immediate root cause diagnosis when metrics shift.
Try: Simulate query distribution drift by evaluating an existing RAG system against out-of-domain queries; measure how retrieval recall and answer confidence degrade as semantic distance increases.
